etymology: From Paul's charge in Ephesians 4:29, "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" — Greek logos sapros, "rotten speech," the same word used of bad fruit and putrid fish; the measure of clean speech is not a list of taboo syllables but whether it edifies.
biblical_def: Corrupt communication is the KJV's phrase for rotten speech (Eph 4:29). Its definition in this dictionary is a doctrine the age desperately needs: God locates the sin of the tongue in the heart's intent, not in a culture's list of forbidden syllables. The standard Paul gives is not a word-bank but a purpose — "that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers." Two truths follow, and most people hold only one. First, the smoothest words can be utterly corrupt: "the words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords" (Psa 55:21). "Bless your heart" can be hissed with the venom of a curse; flattery, gossip dressed as a prayer request, and the polished half-truth are corrupt communication though no four-letter word appears. Second, sharp and even coarse words can be righteous when the heart is right and the target is arrogant evil: Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal (1 Kgs 18:27), Paul wished the circumcision-party would emasculate themselves (Gal 5:12) and counted his own righteousness as dung (Phil 3:8). So the syllable is not the seat of sin; the heart is — for "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" (Matt 12:34), and the Word judges "the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Heb 4:12). Culture does not make a word clean or filthy. God does.
webster_summary: Eph 4:29 — rotten speech, measured not by a syllable-taboo but by whether it edifies. The heart, not the word, is the seat of sin: smooth words can be drawn swords (Psa 55:21); sharp words can be righteous (1 Kgs 18:27). God weighs the thoughts and intents of the heart (Heb 4:12).
webster_full: CORRUPT COMMUNICATION, noun phrase (Eph 4:29). Rotten or worthless speech; Greek logos sapros, used of bad fruit and putrid fish.
The test is purpose, not vocabulary: speech "good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."
Therefore smooth, polite, or pious words can be corrupt (flattery, gossip, the contemptuous "bless your heart").
And sharp, even coarse, words can be clean when the heart is right and the target is arrogant evil (Elijah; Paul).
The seat of the sin is the heart (Matt 12:34), which God alone reads (Heb 4:12) — culture does not set the standard.
scriptures: Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Matt 12:36
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.
Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: The age errs in both directions: the libertine says "it's only a word, my heart is fine" to license cruelty and coarseness, while the pharisee polices syllables and never examines the heart — both deny Matthew 12, which puts the heart, not the dictionary, on trial.
corruption_paragraphs: The libertine error — "just a word." The modern defense of every coarse or cutting thing is "relax, it's only a word; my heart is fine." But Scripture's standard is edification and grace to the hearer (Eph 4:29), and that standard is not met by intent alone. A word whose ordinary use degrades the weak is not sanctified by a clever heart: the LORD forbids cursing the deaf and tripping the blind (Lev 19:14) and warns that "whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker" (Prov 17:5). The prophetic taunt that this dictionary honors — Elijah against Baal, Paul against the Judaizers — is always aimed UP, at arrogant power and idolatry, never DOWN at the disabled, the child, or the broken. And collapsing a real category of sin into a generic insult does not exalt the category; it cheapens it. So the heart-principle cuts toward liberty AND toward love, and a man who only hears the liberty has not heard it.

The pharisaical error — syllable-policing. The opposite mistake makes a religion of vocabulary: it gasps at a blunt word while trafficking in contempt, slander, and the murderous-sweet "bless your heart." The Lord reserved His hardest words for exactly this respectable corruption — whited sepulchres, clean outsides over dead insides (Matt 23:27). The cure for both errors is the same and it is not a longer banned-words list: it is a new heart whose abundance is grace, so that the mouth, given liberty, spends it on building up. Weigh the heart and weigh the hearer. Is it true? Is it for edifying? Does it wither the proud or wound the weak? That — not the culture's shifting taboo — is the measure of clean speech.
roots_summary: Greek logos sapros (Eph 4:29), "rotten speech" — the same sapros used of bad fruit (Matt 7:17) and worthless fish (Matt 13:48); the opposite is speech that edifies and ministers grace.
roots_lines: Sapros also describes bad fruit (Matt 7:17) and bad fish (Matt 13:48)
The measure given is oikodome — building up, edification (Eph 4:29)
Heart-root: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt 12:34)
Judged by the One who discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart (Heb 4:12)
usage: Corrupt communication is measured by Eph 4:29's question — does it edify? — not by a list of forbidden syllables.
His words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords (Psa 55:21): the politest sentence can be the rottenest.
The heart is on trial, not the dictionary — God weighs the thoughts and intents (Heb 4:12).

etymology: Scots/British dialect (from fuffle, to dishevel, with a car-/ker- intensifier), in wide informal use through the 20th century; a commotion, fuss, or to-do — usually over something smaller than the noise it generates.
biblical_def: A kerfuffle is a commotion or fuss — the cheerful, slightly comic word for a tempest in a teapot, a flap, a to-do. It carries its own verdict in its sound: a kerfuffle is, by definition, a disturbance out of proportion to its cause. The dictionary keeps it as a small gift of plain English and notes the wisdom folded into it. Scripture is much occupied with the difference between a real matter and a mere kerfuffle, and with the temperament that can tell them apart. "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Prov 15:1); "the discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Prov 19:11); "be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). Much of what inflames a household, a church, or a comment thread is a kerfuffle — froth that a soft answer would have settled — and the mark of a wise and peaceable man is that he neither manufactures kerfuffles nor is swept into them, but keeps his powder dry for the things that actually matter. To name a thing a kerfuffle is already half to master it.
webster_summary: A commotion or fuss, usually out of proportion to its cause; a flap, a to-do. A plain-English gift — and a reminder that wisdom tells a real matter from froth and answers the froth softly (Prov 15:1; Eccl 7:9).
webster_full: KERFUFFLE, noun (informal). A commotion, fuss, or disturbance, especially one out of proportion to its cause.
From Scots/British dialect fuffle (to dishevel, throw into disorder) with an intensifying prefix.
A flap, a to-do, a tempest in a teapot; carries a faintly comic, deflating tone.
To call a dispute a kerfuffle is to judge it small — froth, not substance.
Wisdom's use: distinguish a real matter from a kerfuffle, and answer the froth softly (Prov 15:1).
scriptures: Prov 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Prov 19:11
The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
Eccl 7:9
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
Prov 17:14
The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with.
corruption_summary: Kerfuffle needs no defense from redefinition; its quiet lesson is the wisdom that distinguishes a real matter from froth and refuses to be swept into a fuss.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is proportion. A great deal of the noise that wrecks peace — in marriages, churches, and the endless comment-thread of the age — is kerfuffle: a disturbance far larger than its cause, which a soft answer (Prov 15:1) would have quieted before it spread. The discretion of a man defers his anger, and it is his glory to pass over a transgression (Prov 19:11).

The deflating word is a tool of peace. To name a flap a kerfuffle is already to refuse it the dignity of a war; it is the verbal equivalent of leaving off contention before it is meddled with, while the breach is still as small as a trickle of water (Prov 17:14). The peaceable man neither manufactures kerfuffles to feel important nor is swept into other men's, but saves his strength for the things that are not froth — the truth of the gospel, the good of souls, the honor of God.
roots_summary: Scots/British dialect fuffle (to dishevel) with a ker- intensifier; a commotion out of proportion to its cause — froth a soft answer settles (Prov 15:1).
roots_lines: Scots/British dialect fuffle — to dishevel, throw into disorder
Sense: a commotion, fuss, or to-do, usually over a small matter
Faintly comic, deflating tone — names a dispute as froth
Wisdom-kin: the soft answer, the deferred anger, the passed-over offense
usage: "The whole kerfuffle over the seating chart" — a flap larger than its cause.
A soft answer turneth away wrath (Prov 15:1): most kerfuffles die at the first gentle word.
The wise man neither starts kerfuffles nor is swept into them; he saves his strength for what is not froth.

etymology: From the "-maxxing" suffix family (looksmaxxing, mewing) = to maximize a trait; popularized in 2025-26 tech-and-podcast circles (notably venture capitalist Marc Andreessen on the David Senra podcast) as a deliberately provocative name for anti-introspection — "stop ruminating, just act."
biblical_def: Retardmaxxing is a deliberately provocative internet and tech-culture term for the practice of NOT over-thinking: doing what needs to be done, refusing to ruminate, and prizing action over endless self-analysis. Despite the crude name (built on the "-maxxing" suffix, like looksmaxxing), the actual idea — popularized by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen on the David Senra podcast, and echoed by figures like Dana White — is a reaction against modern therapy-and-rumination culture: in Andreessen's framing, great men of history did not sit around introspecting, and we need more action and less introspection. The dictionary weighs it honestly, because Scripture cuts both ways. There IS a true insight here: faith is active, not merely reflective — "be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves" (Jas 1:22); the sluggard talks while the diligent works, for "in all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" (Prov 14:23); and a morbid, Christ-less introspection that only circles the self is a real snare. BUT the wholesale contempt for self-examination is itself unbiblical, for God commands it: "examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5); "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psa 139:23); "let a man examine himself" at the Lord's table (1 Cor 11:28). The Christian mean is examination that drives to Christ and out into obedience — neither the navel-gazing the term rightly mocks nor the unexamined life it wrongly commends. (On whether the coarse name itself is sin, see corrupt communication — and note the irony of a movement against thought branding itself with a slur for the unintelligent.)
webster_summary: Provocatively-named tech-culture term (Marc Andreessen, via the David Senra podcast) for anti-rumination — "less introspection, more action." A true insight (Jas 1:22, be doers) wrapped in a coarse name and an over-correction against the self-examination God commands (2 Cor 13:5). Verdict: examine.
webster_full: RETARDMAXXING, n./v. (internet / tech-culture slang, c. 2025-26) Deliberately not over-thinking; prizing action over rumination and self-analysis.
From the "-maxxing" suffix (looksmaxxing, mewing) = maximize a trait; here, provocatively, "maximize not-overthinking."
Popularized by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen on the David Senra podcast; echoed by figures like Dana White.
A reaction against therapy / rumination culture: more action, less introspection.
Decoded by Scripture's two-edged word: be doers (Jas 1:22), yet examine yourselves (2 Cor 13:5).
scriptures: Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
Prov 14:23
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
corruption_summary: The term smuggles a half-truth: it rightly rebukes Christ-less, action-less rumination, but wrongly despises the self-examination God commands. The coarse name — a slur for the unintelligent — is its own tell (see corrupt communication).
corruption_paragraphs: The half it gets right. Against a culture that can analyze its feelings forever and obey nothing, "less introspection, more action" lands a real blow. Scripture has no patience for faith that is all reflection and no obedience: be doers of the word, not hearers only (Jas 1:22); faith without works is dead (Jas 2:26); and the talk of the lips tends only to penury while labour profits (Prov 14:23). Endless morbid introspection that never looks OFF self and TO Christ is a snare the Puritans knew well — the cure for much spiritual paralysis is duty done in faith, not one more lap around the self.

The half it gets wrong. But the wholesale scorn of self-examination is not wisdom; it is the opposite ditch. God commands the examined life: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith (2 Cor 13:5); search me, O God (Psa 139:23); let a man examine himself before the table (1 Cor 11:28); commune with your own heart upon your bed (Psa 4:4). The biblical mean is examination aimed at repentance and obedience — it looks inward in order to look up, and then to go out. And the coarse name preaches its own sermon: a movement against thought branding itself with a slur for the unintelligent says more than it means (see corrupt communication; Lev 19:14).
roots_summary: The "-maxxing" suffix (maximize a trait) + a provocative anti-intellectual flourish; coined in 2025-26 tech/podcast culture (Marc Andreessen, David Senra) for anti-rumination — "more action, less introspection."
roots_lines: "-maxxing" suffix family: looksmaxxing, mewing — to maximize a trait
Popularized by Marc Andreessen on the David Senra podcast (c. 2025-26)
Echoed by figures like Dana White: action over public rumination
Decoded two-edged: be doers (Jas 1:22), yet examine yourselves (2 Cor 13:5)
usage: "He stopped analyzing and just shipped it — full retardmaxxing." The insight: be a doer (Jas 1:22).
It rightly mocks Christ-less rumination, but wrongly scorns the self-examination God commands (2 Cor 13:5).
The biblical mean: examine yourself in order to repent and obey — look in, to look up, then go out.
